neurological_exam.mental_status: GCS 9 (E2V3M4). Minimally responsive. Does not follow commands. Eye opening to pain. Incomprehensible sounds. Purposeful withdrawal to pain. Asterixis cannot be assessed — GCS too low. Girlfriend reports he had a convulsive event 30 minutes before ambulance called.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 4 mm, equal, sluggishly reactive. Doll's eye reflex intact. No nystagmus.
neurological_exam.motor: Minimal spontaneous movement. Purposeful withdrawal pain.
neurological_exam.reflexes: DTRs 1+ bilaterally. Plantar responses extensor (Babinski) bilaterally.
neurological_exam.additional: GCS 9 — severely depressed consciousness after witnessed convulsive episode. Tongue laceration noted. Urinary incontinence during episode. Bilateral extensor plantar responses suggest post-ictal state or severe cerebral dysfunction. This could be: (1) prolonged postictal state from new seizure in known seizure disorder, (2) non-convulsive status epilepticus (NCSE) after seizure, (3) severe HE (grade IV) presenting with GCS 9, or (4) any combination.

patient.chief_complaint: Unresponsive after witnessed seizure — NCSE vs severe HE vs combined
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. F. is a 44-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis, prior seizure disorder treated with levetiracetam, and an established HE prophylaxis regimen, who was brought by ambulance in an unresponsive state. His girlfriend witnessed him having a generalized tonic-clonic seizure approximately 30 minutes before EMS arrival. He had been increasingly confused over the prior 2-3 days — she attributed it to usual HE episodes which he has had twice before. On the morning of presentation, he was more confused than usual, and then she found him on the floor seizing. He had been compliant with rifaximin and lactulose. He is 1 year sober. His levetiracetam had been recently increased from 500 mg BID to 1000 mg BID by his neurologist 3 weeks ago — girlfriend reports he may have missed some doses in the past week ('he kept forgetting'). The clinical puzzle: (1) known seizure disorder — was this a breakthrough seizure from levetiracetam non-adherence? (2) Known HE risk — is the ongoing unresponsiveness (GCS 9) from post-ictal state, NCSE, or severe grade IV HE? (3) EEG is the critical diagnostic test — must exclude NCSE; (4) ammonia will help differentiate HE from post-ictal; (5) levetiracetam level matters. NCSE can present as unresponsive state mimicking grade IV HE and requires urgent EEG diagnosis and treatment.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Non-convulsive status epilepticus (NCSE) following breakthrough generalized tonic-clonic seizure (from subtherapeutic levetiracetam 8 µg/mL due to missed doses) + concurrent severe hepatic encephalopathy (ammonia 108) — both lowering consciousness to GCS 9

Ammonia 108 with cirrhosis — severe HE present and contributing; but EEG shows NCSE not HE triphasic waves; GCS 9 is from NCSE primarily with HE contributing; EEG distinguishes the two
Serum ethanol negative; 1 year sober confirmed; no CIWA symptoms — breakthrough seizure from antiepileptic non-adherence, not alcohol withdrawal

HE lowers seizure threshold — hyperammonemia impairs GABAergic neurotransmission; HE and NCSE are synergistic; treat BOTH simultaneously

key_reasoning_points: GCS 9 after generalized tonic-clonic seizure should NOT be assumed post-ictal — EEG must exclude NCSE; post-ictal states improve within 30-60 min; sustained GCS 9 at 30+ min demands EEG
NCSE can be a complication of breakthrough seizures AND can be facilitated by HE — hyperammonemia lowers seizure threshold; HE + NCSE can coexist
Subtherapeutic antiepileptic levels are a common precipitant of breakthrough seizures — levetiracetam level 8 µg/mL (therapeutic 20-40) confirms non-adherence
EEG distinguishes HE triphasic waves from NCSE spike-wave — CRITICALLY different patterns requiring different treatments; getting EEG early changes management
